P4Q1.q: According to Aquinas, why is it fitting for God to become incarnate?
options: Because it belongs to the essence of goodness to communicate itself to others in the highest way possible
Because God needed a body to interact physically with creation
Because the angels petitioned God on behalf of fallen humanity
Because the Old Testament prophets demanded a visible sign
P4Q1.explanation: Aquinas argues that God's nature is goodness, and it belongs to the essence of goodness to diffuse and communicate itself to others; the Incarnation is the highest form of this self-communication, uniting Word, soul, and flesh in one Person.

P4Q1.q: Was it strictly necessary (in the sense that the end could not otherwise be attained) for God to become incarnate to restore human nature?
options: No, God could have restored human nature many other ways, but Incarnation was the most fitting and convenient way
Yes, God's omnipotence was insufficient without the Incarnation
No, restoration was already complete before the Incarnation
Yes, because only a human being can satisfy for human sin in any way
P4Q1.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes two senses of necessity: absolute necessity (without which an end cannot be reached) and necessity for a better, more fitting attainment of an end. Incarnation was necessary only in the second sense; God could have restored humanity otherwise, but this was the fittest way.

P4Q1.q: On the question of why Christ came chiefly to address original sin rather than merely actual sins, what distinction does Aquinas draw?
options: Original sin is greater 'extensively' since it infects the whole human race, even though actual sin can be greater 'intensively' as more voluntary
Original sin is a lesser evil, so Christ addressed it only incidentally
Actual sin alone required a remedy since original sin carries no real culpability
There is no meaningful distinction; both are equally addressed for identical reasons
P4Q1.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes intensive greatness (actual sin is more voluntary, hence intensively greater) from extensive greatness (original sin affects the whole race, hence extensively greater); Christ came principally to remedy original sin because the good of the whole race is more divine than the good of one person.

P4Q2.q: Where, according to Aquinas, did the union of God and man in Christ properly take place?
options: In the person or hypostasis, not in the nature
In the nature, producing a single mixed nature
In an accidental property, like a garment worn over the Word
In the will alone, through agreement of intentions
P4Q2.explanation: Aquinas rejects union 'in the nature' (which would confuse Godhead and manhood, as Eutyches held) and insists the union occurred in the person/hypostasis of the Word, who subsists in two complete and distinct natures.

P4Q2.q: Why does Aquinas reject the view that the human nature assumed by the Word has its own personality or hypostasis?
options: Because whatever exists not by itself but in something more perfect (the Person of the Word) does not constitute a separate person, just as a hand is not itself a person
Because Christ's human nature was not truly individual
Because personhood requires a body only, not a rational soul
Because the Council of Nicaea explicitly forbade discussing Christ's human personhood
P4Q2.explanation: Aquinas explains that an individual substance is a person only if it subsists by itself; Christ's human nature, though individual, subsists in the Person of the Word rather than on its own, so it does not have its own personality, just as a hand or foot is an individual but not a person.

P4Q2.q: How does Aquinas characterize the union of the human nature to the Word regarding accidents?
options: It is not an accidental union but occurred in the subsistence or hypostasis, a middle position between confusing the natures and merely accidental union (as Nestorius held)
It is purely accidental, like a person putting on clothing with no deeper unity
It is a union in essence, making Godhead and manhood the same nature
It is a merely verbal or nominal union with no real ontological basis
P4Q2.explanation: Aquinas identifies two condemned extremes—Eutyches/Dioscorus confusing the natures, and Nestorius holding an accidental union (indwelling, agreement of wills, etc.)—and affirms the Catholic middle position: union in hypostasis, which is substantial, not accidental.

P4Q3.q: According to Aquinas, is it more proper to say a Divine Person assumes human nature, or that the Divine Nature assumes it?
options: Primarily a Person assumes, since a Person is both principle (by the shared Divine power) and term (since union occurs in the Person) of the assumption; the Nature is said to assume only secondarily
Only the Divine Nature assumes, since Persons cannot act
Only the Father can be said to assume, since He alone is unbegotten
Neither; assumption applies only to the human nature, which assumes divinity
P4Q3.explanation: Aquinas explains assumption involves a principle (the common Divine power) and a term (the Person in whom the human nature subsists); since the term of the union is a Person, assuming is most properly attributed to a Person, though the Nature may be said to assume secondarily as the source of the act.

P4Q3.q: Could the Father or the Holy Spirit, rather than the Son, have become incarnate, according to Aquinas?
options: Yes, since the Divine power common to all three Persons could terminate the union in any Person, though it was most fitting that the Son assumed flesh
No, only the Son possesses the power required for Incarnation
No, because only the Son has a body eternally prepared for assumption
Yes, but only the Holy Spirit, since the Spirit alone sanctifies
P4Q3.explanation: Aquinas holds that since the Divine power and personhood are common to all three Persons, any of them could have assumed human nature; nevertheless it was especially fitting that the Son, the Word (exemplar likeness of all creatures and of wisdom), be the one who did so.

P4Q3.q: Why does Aquinas say it was most fitting that specifically the Person of the Son become incarnate?
options: Because the Word, as the eternal exemplar/concept by which creatures are made, has a special affinity to creatures and especially to rational, wisdom-seeking human nature
Because the Son alone among the Persons has compassion for sinners
Because the Father had already been revealed sufficiently in the Old Testament
Because incarnation requires generation, which only the Son can undergo
P4Q3.explanation: Aquinas argues the Word, as the Father's eternal concept and exemplar likeness of all creation, has particular affinity with human nature (which is perfected through wisdom); thus restoring humanity to its exemplar through personal union with the Word was especially fitting.

P4Q4.q: Why, according to Aquinas, was human nature (rather than angelic or irrational nature) uniquely 'assumable' by the Word?
options: Because human nature alone combines the dignity of a rational nature capable of knowing and loving God with the need for restoration from sin
Because humans are physically similar to God in bodily form
Because angels are too perfect to need any assumption
Because irrational creatures already possess a share in divinity
P4Q4.explanation: Aquinas finds fittingness for assumption in both dignity (rational capacity to know and love the Word) and need (need of restoration from sin); irrational creatures lack the dignity, and angels lack the need, so only human nature has both.

P4Q4.q: Did the Son of God assume a human person, according to Aquinas?
options: No; a human person would have to pre-exist the union as its own hypostasis, but Christ's human nature is not a separate person, only reaching personhood in union with the Word
Yes, and that human person was later dissolved by grace
Yes, and this created a second, distinct person alongside the Word
No, because the Son assumed only a body without a complete human nature
P4Q4.explanation: Aquinas reasons that what is 'assumed' must be presupposed to the assumption, but a human person would either have to be corrupted (uselessly) or persist alongside the Word (yielding two persons, which is false); therefore no human person, only human nature, was assumed.

P4Q4.q: Why did the Son of God assume human nature from the sinful stock of Adam rather than creating a fresh, unrelated human nature?
options: Because justice suggested the offending nature should provide the remedy, it increases human dignity that the conqueror of the devil arose from the very race he conquered, and it manifests God's power in raising a corrupt nature to glory
Because no other matter was available to God for forming a body
Because Adam's nature was already sinless at its root
Because it was administratively simpler for genealogical purposes only
P4Q4.explanation: Aquinas, citing Augustine, gives three reasons: justice (the guilty nature makes amends), dignity (the devil is conquered by one from the very race he defeated), and manifest divine power (elevating a corrupt nature to great glory).

P4Q5.q: Why does Aquinas insist Christ assumed a true, real (not imaginary or heavenly) body?
options: Because human nature by definition requires a true body, His true suffering and death required real flesh, and it befits the Truth Himself to have nothing fictitious in His work
Because Scripture nowhere claims Christ had a body at all
Because only a heavenly body could perform miracles
Because Roman law required physical proof of birth for legal personhood
P4Q5.explanation: Aquinas gives three reasons for a true body: the essence of human nature requires true flesh, the reality of Christ's sufferings and death (and thus our salvation) depends on it, and it befits Christ as Truth itself to have nothing merely apparent about Him.

P4Q5.q: According to Aquinas, why did the Son of God need to assume not just a soul, but specifically a rational mind/intellect (against the Apollinarian view that the Word replaced the human mind)?
options: Because Scripture shows Christ marveling (which requires a mind), the mind is where sin and justifying grace properly reside so it needed saving, and without a mind the assumed flesh would not truly be human flesh
Because a mind was needed only so Christ could perform miracles
Because Apollinaris agreed the Word could not replace bodily functions
Because the human mind is superior to the Divine intellect and thus needed no assumption
P4Q5.explanation: Aquinas rebuts Apollinaris using Gospel evidence of Christ marveling (implying a real human mind), the fact that sin and grace pertain to the mind (so redemption required a mind), and the principle that flesh without a rational soul/mind would not be true human flesh.

P4Q5.q: What is Aquinas's key argument for why Christ needed a genuine human soul, not merely the Word functioning in place of a soul?
options: Scripture attributes true soul-acts to Christ (sorrow, an offered life), the utility of the Incarnation requires the soul itself to be healed, and flesh only becomes human flesh through the presence of a rational soul
The soul was unnecessary since salvation concerns the body alone
Only the body needed redemption, per Manichean teaching
The Word could not truly suffer without abandoning divinity, so a soul was substituted entirely
P4Q5.explanation: Against Arius and Apollinaris (who held the Word replaced the soul), Aquinas argues from Scripture (Christ's soul is sorrowful, His soul is laid down), from the point of redemption (the soul itself needed healing), and from the metaphysics of human nature (flesh is only truly 'flesh' through ensoulment).

P4Q6.q: In what sense does Aquinas say the Word assumed flesh 'through the medium of the soul'?
options: In the order of dignity and causality, the soul ranks between God and flesh, and flesh is only assumable as human flesh because of its relation to the rational soul
In a temporal sense, meaning the soul was assumed noticeably earlier than the flesh
Only metaphorically, with no real ordering intended
Because the soul physically carries the flesh into existence over time
P4Q6.explanation: Aquinas clarifies there is no temporal 'medium' since soul and body were united simultaneously in Christ; rather, in the order of dignity and of causality the soul is 'between' God and flesh, and flesh is assumable only because of its ordering to the rational soul.

P4Q6.q: Did the Word assume Christ's soul before assuming his flesh, according to Aquinas?
options: No; the soul and body were assumed simultaneously, since a soul is not fittingly united to the Word prior to being united to a body (as with all human souls)
Yes, Origen's view that the soul pre-existed and was later joined to flesh is affirmed as correct
Yes, but only for a few days during the first trimester
No, the flesh was assumed centuries before the soul, at the time of Adam
P4Q6.explanation: Aquinas rejects Origen's view that souls (including Christ's) pre-exist their bodies; Christ's soul, like every human soul, is created at the same time it is infused into the body, so soul and flesh were assumed together, not sequentially.

P4Q6.q: According to Aquinas, does grace serve as a 'medium' through which the human nature was assumed by the Word?
options: No; the grace of union is itself the very term of the assumption (not a means to it), while habitual grace is an effect that follows the union, not its medium
Yes, habitual grace was the instrumental cause that made the union possible
Yes, both graces served jointly as the efficient medium of assumption
No, because grace played no role whatsoever in the Incarnation
P4Q6.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the grace of union (the very gratuitous personal union itself, hence the term rather than a means of assumption) from habitual grace (which is a consequence flowing from the union, per John 1:14); neither functions as a 'medium' of assumption in the ordinary sense.

P4Q7.q: Why does Aquinas hold that Christ's soul possessed habitual grace, not merely the grace of union?
options: Because nearness to the source of grace (the Word), the dignity of a soul destined for the closest knowledge and love of God, and Christ's role as Mediator overflowing grace to others all required it
Because habitual grace is identical to the grace of union and thus automatically present
Because Christ needed habitual grace only to perform miracles, not for personal holiness
Because the human soul cannot exist at all without habitual grace by natural necessity
P4Q7.explanation: Aquinas gives three reasons: closeness to the source of grace increases participation in it, the soul's operations of knowing and loving God at the highest level require grace, and Christ's mediatorial role required grace that would overflow to others.

P4Q7.q: Why did Aquinas conclude that Christ, despite having all other virtues, did not have the virtue of faith?
options: Because faith's object is a Divine thing not seen, but from the first moment of His conception Christ saw the Divine Essence, so what is seen cannot be an object of faith for Him
Because faith is a virtue exclusively for the underprivileged
Because Christ's teaching role made having faith redundant socially, though not logically impossible
Because Aquinas holds Christ definitely did possess faith, contrary to how the question is usually summarized
P4Q7.explanation: Since faith by definition concerns what is not seen, and Christ possessed the beatific vision (seeing the Divine Essence) from the first instant of His conception, the very object of faith was absent for Him, so faith properly speaking could not be in Him.

P4Q7.q: How does Aquinas explain the sense in which Christ possessed the fulness of grace?
options: Both intensively (grace in the highest degree possible) and extensively/in power (extending to all its effects, as grace was to overflow from Him to others)
Only extensively, since His grace was actually quite moderate in intensity
Only intensively, since His grace did not extend or overflow to others
Neither; 'fulness of grace' is purely a title of honor with no real theological content
P4Q7.explanation: Aquinas argues Christ has fulness of grace in two ways: intensively, because His nearness to the source of grace (God) means He receives it in the highest possible degree, and 'as regards power,' because grace was given to Him precisely so that it could overflow to all others, like fire that is hottest and also causes heat in other things.

P4Q8.q: What three things does Aquinas identify in a physical 'head' that ground the metaphor of Christ as Head of the Church?
options: Order (first part), perfection (seat of all the senses), and power (source of movement/direction for the other members)
Size, color, and shape
Location, temperature, and weight
Visibility, mobility, and symmetry
P4Q8.explanation: Aquinas draws the analogy from the physical head's order (topmost/first part), perfection (all senses gathered there), and power (directing movement of the other members), and argues Christ has each of these spiritually: nearness to God, fulness of grace, and power to bestow grace on others.

P4Q8.q: According to Aquinas, is Christ the Head only of human souls, or of bodies too?
options: Of both souls and bodies, though principally souls (through justifying grace) and secondarily bodies (through the resurrection/glorification that flows from the soul)
Of bodies only, since souls are governed directly by the Holy Spirit alone
Of neither; 'Head' is purely a metaphor without real causal influence
Of souls only; Christ's headship has no bearing on bodily resurrection
P4Q8.explanation: Aquinas reasons the body serves the soul as its instrument, so Christ's headship principally reaches souls (through grace) but also extends secondarily to bodies, since glory eventually flows from the soul to the body, as in the resurrection.

P4Q8.q: Does Aquinas hold that Christ is Head of the angels as well as of men?
options: Yes, because angels and men together form one mystical body ordained to the same end (the glory of Divine fruition), and Christ shares divine gifts even more fully than the angels do
No, angels have their own independent head distinct from Christ
No, since only embodied creatures can belong to a 'head-body' relationship
Yes, but only of fallen angels, as a form of punishment
P4Q8.explanation: Aquinas argues that since angels and men are both ordained to the one end of beatific glory, they form one mystical body, and since Christ is nearer to God and receives divine gifts even more fully than angels, He is Head of angels as well as of men.

P4Q9.q: Why, according to Aquinas, did Christ need created (not merely Divine) knowledge?
options: Because His soul, in potentiality to intelligible things, needed to be perfected and actualized; a rational soul is for the sake of understanding; and natural knowledge of first principles belongs to human nature which He fully assumed
Because the Divine knowledge in Christ was somehow deficient or incomplete
Because created knowledge is superior in every way to Divine knowledge
Because the human soul cannot exist unless it is currently exercising some act of knowledge at every moment
P4Q9.explanation: Aquinas argues Christ's soul, like any human soul, starts in potentiality regarding intelligible things and would be imperfect unless actualized by knowledge; furthermore, a rational soul exists for the sake of understanding, and human nature naturally includes knowledge of first principles, all of which Christ fully possessed.

P4Q9.q: According to Aquinas, why was it necessary for Christ to have the beatific vision (the knowledge of the blessed/comprehensors)?
options: Because Christ leads humanity to the end of beatitude, and a cause must be at least as perfect as the effect it produces, so He who brings others to the vision of God must possess it Himself pre-eminently
Because the beatific vision is required merely for moral perfection, not causal headship
Because without it Christ could not have a human body at all
Because the beatific vision was granted only after His Resurrection, not from conception
P4Q9.explanation: Aquinas reasons that Christ's humanity is the means by which humans are brought to beatific glory (Hebrews 2:10), and since a cause must be more efficacious than its effect, Christ must possess the beatific vision pre-eminently from the outset.

P4Q9.q: What is 'acquired' (empiric) knowledge in Christ, and why does Aquinas affirm Christ possessed it, revising an earlier view of his own?
options: Knowledge gained naturally through the active intellect abstracting from sense experience (phantasms); Aquinas affirms it because nothing planted by God in human nature, including the active intellect's proper operation, was lacking in Christ
Knowledge given directly by angels appearing to Christ in visions
Knowledge that Christ acquired only after His Ascension into heaven
A form of knowledge Aquinas denies Christ ever possessed, contrary to common claims
P4Q9.explanation: Aquinas explains that since Christ's human nature included an active intellect (whose proper operation is abstracting intelligible species from phantasms), and nothing would exist in Him in vain, He must have had genuinely acquired/empiric knowledge; Aquinas notes he had written differently in an earlier work but corrects himself here.

P4Q10.q: According to Aquinas, did the soul of Christ 'comprehend' (fully grasp) the Divine Essence?
options: No; no creature can comprehend the infinite Divine Essence, since the finite cannot comprehend the infinite, even though Christ's soul truly sees that Essence
Yes, because hypostatic union grants comprehension automatically
No, because Christ's soul never saw the Divine Essence at all, only a created likeness of it
Yes, but only after the Ascension, not during His earthly life
P4Q10.explanation: Aquinas is careful to distinguish 'seeing' from 'comprehending': although Christ's human soul truly sees the Divine Essence (the beatific vision), it cannot comprehend it, since the finite creature cannot fully grasp the infinite God.

P4Q10.q: Does Christ's soul, in Aquinas's view, know 'all things' in the Word, including everything merely possible that God could bring about but never will?
options: He knows in the Word all things that are, were, or will be, and all that lies within the power of any creature, but not the entire infinite scope of what lies solely within God's power, since that would require comprehending the Divine Essence itself
Yes, without qualification, Christ's soul knows absolutely everything God could ever possibly do
No, Christ's soul knows only what happened during His own lifetime on earth
No, Christ's human soul has no vision of the Word at all, only ordinary human knowledge
P4Q10.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes 'all things' actually occurring across time (which Christ's soul knows in the Word) from the unlimited things possible to God's power alone (which would require comprehending God's infinite power/essence, impossible for a creature); but Christ does know all that lies within creaturely power, even unrealized possibilities.

P4Q10.q: Why does Aquinas say Christ's soul sees the Divine Essence more clearly/perfectly than any other creature?
options: Because His soul is united to the Word in person, making it more closely joined to the Word than any other creature, and thus receiving the light of glory more fully
Because Christ's soul, unlike other blessed souls, does not need the light of glory to see God
Because other blessed creatures see a lesser, created substitute for the Divine Essence, while Christ alone sees the real one
Because clarity of vision depends solely on merit accumulated during earthly life, and Christ lived longest in grace
P4Q10.explanation: Aquinas reasons that all the blessed see God through a participated light flowing from the Word, but since Christ's soul is personally/hypostatically united to the Word itself, it receives this illuminating light more fully than any other creature, and so sees the Divine Essence most perfectly.

P4Q11.q: According to Aquinas, could Christ use His infused (imprinted) knowledge by turning to phantasms, as ordinary human knowers do?
options: No; Christ's soul had the condition of a comprehensor, which is not dependent on the body or on turning to phantasms, unlike a wayfarer's soul
Yes, exactly as any other human being must, with no difference
No, because Christ had no body capable of producing phantasms
Yes, but only during His infancy before the age of reason
P4Q11.explanation: Aquinas explains that a comprehensor's soul dominates the body rather than depending on it, and Christ's soul, having the beatific vision from conception, had the conditions of a comprehensor, so it did not need to turn to phantasms as wayfaring souls do.

P4Q11.q: How does Aquinas compare Christ's infused knowledge to angelic knowledge?
options: It surpassed angelic knowledge in what it received from its divine source (extent and certainty), but fell short of angels in the human, phantasm-based mode of receiving and using it
It was inferior to angelic knowledge in every respect, since angels are naturally superior beings
It was identical to angelic knowledge in mode and degree, since both are infused
It exceeded angelic knowledge in every respect including its natural mode of operation
P4Q11.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the source (the light imprinted on Christ's soul is more excellent than angelic light, so Christ's knowledge surpasses the angels' in content and certainty) from the mode of reception (Christ's soul, being human, naturally knows by turning to phantasms and discursive reasoning, a mode inferior to the angels' connatural mode).

P4Q11.q: Was Christ's infused knowledge organized as a single undifferentiated habit, or as multiple distinct habits?
options: Multiple distinct habits, since it is connatural to the human soul (unlike angels) to receive less universal species and know different subject-classes through different habits of knowledge
A single simple habit, mirroring the simplicity of angelic knowledge
No habit at all, since it had to be re-infused for each act of understanding
It was not a form of knowledge at all, but pure will
P4Q11.explanation: Aquinas argues that because it is connatural to the human soul to receive less universal intelligible species than angels do, and different classes of knowable objects correspond to different habits of science, Christ's infused knowledge was accordingly divided into distinct habits.

P4Q12.q: Why does Aquinas affirm that Christ genuinely 'advanced' in knowledge and grace as He grew, despite already having the fulness of grace and infused knowledge from the first instant?
options: The advancement was in effect, not in essence: with the same habitual knowledge, He increasingly demonstrated greater deeds and manifested knowledge and grace as His age allowed, especially in acquired/empiric knowledge
The advancement was purely essential, meaning His grace literally increased in degree over time
There was no real advancement at all; Scripture's language about His growth is purely figurative
He advanced only in bodily strength, never in any form of knowledge
P4Q12.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes advancement 'in essence' (an increased habit) from advancement 'in effect' (the same habit progressively manifesting itself in greater acts); Christ's growth in wisdom and stature is understood in the second sense, particularly regarding His acquired knowledge.

P4Q12.q: Did Christ, according to Aquinas, learn anything from a human teacher?
options: No; as the Head of the Church established by God to teach all others the truth, it did not befit His dignity to be taught by any man
Yes, He learned the Law extensively from the rabbis in the Temple as a source of new truth
Yes, His mother Mary was formally His only teacher in all matters
No, because He had no acquired knowledge whatsoever to be taught
P4Q12.explanation: Aquinas reasons that as the first mover in a genus is not moved by that same kind of motion, and Christ is established as Head and chief teacher of all, giving testimony to the truth, it did not befit Him to receive teaching from any mere man.

P4Q12.q: Did Christ receive knowledge from the angels, in Aquinas's account?
options: He received empiric knowledge of sensible things through His own active intellect (with no need of angelic light), and received infused knowledge directly from the Word rather than through angelic mediation
Yes, all of His infused knowledge came exclusively through angelic illumination, exactly as with other humans
No, He received no knowledge whatsoever apart from the beatific vision
Yes, but only knowledge of future events, delivered by the angel Gabriel
P4Q12.explanation: Aquinas holds that Christ's soul, being united to the Word in the unity of person, received its higher infused knowledge directly from the Word itself rather than through the mediation of angels (unlike other humans, who may receive illumination via angels), while His empiric knowledge came through His own active intellect.

P4Q13.q: According to Aquinas, could Christ's human soul, by its own natural power, change His own body outside the ordinary course of nature (e.g., alter its natural disposition at will)?
options: Not by its own proper natural power, since a soul has a determinate natural relation to its own body; only as an instrument united in person to the Word could such power be exercised, and even then the power is attributed to the Word rather than to the soul as such
Yes, His soul had full natural power to alter its own body in any way, with no need of the Word's power
No, His soul had absolutely no power over His body under any description, not even as instrument of the Word
Yes, because the human soul naturally possesses omnipotence over its own body in every human being
P4Q13.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes Christ's soul in its own proper nature and power (limited, like any soul, to a determinate natural relation with its body) from Christ's soul as an instrument united in person to the Word (through which every disposition of His body was subject to divine power, though this omnipotence is attributed properly to the Word, the principal agent, not to the soul as instrument).

P4Q13.q: Regarding the execution of His will, in what sense did Christ's soul have 'omnipotence,' according to Aquinas?
options: Whatever Christ willed to bring about by Himself, He was able to do (fitting His wisdom); but things He willed to be brought about only by Divine power (such as His own resurrection) He could not effect by His own power, only as instrument of the Godhead
Christ's soul could bring about absolutely anything at all by its own proper power, without qualification
Christ's soul had no power to accomplish anything He willed, human or divine
Christ's human will and the Divine will were entirely separate and could not cooperate in any action
P4Q13.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes what Christ's soul willed to do itself (which it was capable of doing, fittingly with His wisdom) from what He willed to be brought about by Divine power alone, such as His resurrection, which He could not effect by His soul's proper power except as instrument of the Godhead.

P4Q14.q: Why, according to Aquinas, was it fitting for Christ to assume bodily defects like hunger, thirst, and death?
options: To satisfy for sin by taking on its punishment in our place, to prove the reality of His human nature against those who denied it, and to give us an example of patience in bearing suffering
Because bodily defects are intrinsically good and perfect human nature
Because without them Christ could not have performed any miracles
Because the Father commanded these defects as an arbitrary test unrelated to sin or example
P4Q14.explanation: Aquinas gives three reasons: satisfaction for sin requires bearing sin's punishment (death, hunger, etc.), assuming real bodily defects proves the truth of His human nature against docetic-type errors, and enduring them models patience for believers.

P4Q14.q: Did Christ, in Aquinas's view, 'contract' bodily defects the way ordinary descendants of Adam do?
options: No; Christ assumed such defects by His own will, not as something owed to Him on account of sin, since He received human nature in the purity it had before the Fall
Yes, exactly as every other human being does, involuntarily and as a consequence of original sin in Him
No, because Christ had no genuine bodily defects at all
Yes, but only the defects of his mother's ancestry, not Adam's
P4Q14.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes 'contracting' a defect (receiving it of necessity as an effect of sin) from voluntarily assuming it; Christ received human nature without sin, as it existed before the Fall, and freely willed to take on defects like death for our sake, rather than contracting them via sin's necessity.

P4Q14.q: Which bodily defects did Christ NOT assume, according to Aquinas?
options: Defects incompatible with the fulness of grace and knowledge (like ignorance or proneness to evil), and particular defects like leprosy caused by individual fault or a defective formative power
All bodily defects whatsoever, since He was without any real human weakness
Only defects related to old age, since He died relatively young
None; He assumed literally every defect any human has ever had, without exception
P4Q14.explanation: Aquinas holds Christ assumed only the common defects flowing from the whole of human nature due to original sin (death, hunger, thirst, and the like) — the 'natural and indetractible passions' — but not defects incompatible with perfect grace/knowledge, nor particular ailments arising from individual fault or defective formation.

P4Q15.q: Why does Aquinas conclude Christ had absolutely no sin, neither original nor actual?
options: Sin would impede satisfaction for others rather than aid it, sin does not belong to the true nature God created (only corrupting it), and sin could not serve as an example of virtue since it opposes virtue
Because sin is impossible for any human nature whatsoever to have, Christ included or not
Because Christ inherited His nature entirely apart from Adam's line, so original sin could not apply regardless of other factors
Because Aquinas actually concludes Christ had actual sin but not original sin
P4Q15.explanation: Aquinas ties this to the three purposes for which Christ assumed human defects (satisfaction, proof of true humanity, and example of virtue); since sin serves none of these purposes but actively opposes them, Christ assumed no sin, citing 1 Peter 2:22 that He did no sin.

P4Q15.q: Did Christ have the 'fomes' (tinder/kindling) of sin — the disordered inclination of the sensitive appetite against reason?
options: No; since Christ had the virtues in their highest degree, and greater virtue increasingly subdues the fomes of sin, in Him the fomes was entirely absent
Yes, to the same degree as in ordinary fallen humans
Yes, but only in a diminished, non-culpable form present in all human souls
No, because Christ lacked a sensitive appetite altogether
P4Q15.explanation: Aquinas reasons that moral virtue subjects the lower appetites to reason in proportion to its perfection; since Christ had the virtues in their highest possible degree, the fomes of sin (whose nature is to incline the sensual appetite against reason) was entirely absent in Him.

P4Q15.q: According to Aquinas, was Christ's soul capable of suffering (passible), including true sensible pain and sorrow?
options: Yes; since His body was passible and mortal and His soul was truly united to it, and since He apprehended things as genuinely hurtful (to Himself and others), He experienced real pain and real sorrow, not merely apparent emotion
No, His soul was entirely impassible from the moment of conception, feeling nothing in the body
Yes for pain, but Aquinas denies He ever experienced sorrow, since sorrow implies imperfection
No, because a comprehensor's soul by definition cannot suffer in any way
P4Q15.explanation: Aquinas affirms real bodily pain (from His passible, mortal body and full natural power of sensation) and real sorrow (from apprehending evils to Himself, like His coming Passion, or to others, like the sins of Judas or the Jews), citing Augustine that Christ assumed true human affections whenever He judged fitting.

P4Q16.q: Why does Aquinas affirm both 'God is man' and 'man is God' as true and proper statements?
options: Because there is one suppositum/hypostasis of both natures (the Person of the Son), so 'man' can stand for that same Person of whom 'God' is also truly predicated
Because 'God' and 'man' are simply synonyms with identical meaning
Because the human nature was itself transformed into the Divine Nature at the Incarnation
Because both statements are actually false in Aquinas's own final judgment
P4Q16.explanation: Aquinas grounds both predications in the single hypostasis of Christ: since the word 'man' can stand for the Person of the Son of God (the one hypostasis of human nature), and 'God' is truly said of that same Person, both 'God is man' and 'man is God' are true and proper.

P4Q16.q: According to Aquinas, is it correct to say 'Christ began to be' without qualification?
options: No; taken simply this is false, since 'this Man' (pointing to Christ) refers to the eternal suppositum (the Person of the Word), with which a temporal beginning is incompatible
Yes, without any qualification needed, since His human nature clearly began in time
Yes, and Aquinas endorses Arius's reasoning that the Son 'began to be'
No, because Aquinas denies Christ ever had a true human nature that could begin
P4Q16.explanation: Aquinas explains that since 'this Man' picks out the eternal suppositum (the Person of the Son), and eternity is incompatible with a temporal beginning, the unqualified statement is false; moreover, using it carelessly risks echoing the condemned Arian claim that the Son 'began to be' and 'was not' at some point.

P4Q16.q: How does Aquinas evaluate the claim 'Christ as Man is God'?
options: It should be denied rather than granted, because the reduplication 'as Man' primarily signifies the nature (which is distinct from the Divine Nature), even though, taken as referring to the suppositum, it is technically true
It is simply and unqualifiedly true with no caveats needed
It is simply and unqualifiedly false in every sense
Aquinas refuses to address this question at all, calling it meaningless
P4Q16.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes two senses of the reduplicative 'as Man': referring to the nature (in which sense the statement is false, since human nature differs from divine) or to the suppositum (in which sense it is true, since the suppositum is the Son of God); but since 'as Man' more properly signifies the nature, the statement should generally be denied.

P4Q17.q: Is Christ 'one' or 'two,' according to Aquinas?
options: One, because although there are two natures in Christ, 'one' and 'two' are predicated according to the suppositum/hypostasis, which is single, not according to the two natures taken abstractly
Two, because there are unambiguously two complete supposita in Christ, divine and human
One, but only in a merely metaphorical or verbal sense with no real unity underlying it
Two, since the human nature can be predicated abstractly of Christ just as the divine nature can
P4Q17.explanation: Aquinas notes that while the divine nature can be predicated of Christ both abstractly and concretely, the human nature can be predicated of Him only concretely (via the suppositum); since numerical predication like 'one' or 'two' tracks the suppositum, and there is only one suppositum in Christ, Christ is rightly called one, not two.

P4Q17.q: Does Aquinas hold that there is only one 'being' (esse) in Christ, corresponding to His one hypostasis?
options: Yes for personal being (which cannot be multiplied in one hypostasis, since one thing has one act of being as itself), though accidental 'beings' (like being white) could in principle be multiplic in one hypostasis
No, Christ has two complete and parallel acts of personal being, one divine and one human, existing side by side
Yes, but Aquinas holds this 'being' is purely human, with the divine being wholly absent
No, being is entirely irrelevant to hypostasis in Aquinas's treatment
P4Q17.explanation: Aquinas reasons that being pertains to the hypostasis as the one who has it, and the personal being of a hypostasis cannot be multiplied, since one thing cannot have more than one act of being as itself; hence there is only one (personal) being in Christ, corresponding to His single hypostasis, unlike accidental features which could in principle be multiple.

P4Q18.q: Against Apollinaris, Eutyches, and the Monothelites (who held Christ's human nature never moved with its own motion), what does Aquinas affirm about the number of wills in Christ?
options: There are two wills in Christ, human and divine, corresponding to His two complete natures
There is only one will in Christ, corresponding to His one Person, exactly as the Monothelites taught
There is no will in Christ at all, only pure divine determination
There are three wills in Christ, one for each nature and one for the hypostasis
P4Q18.explanation: Aquinas rejects the various routes to a single will (denial of a human soul/intellect, one composite nature, or a human nature that never truly moves itself) and affirms two wills in Christ, corresponding to the two complete and distinct natures, human and divine.

P4Q18.q: Was Christ's human will, in its 'will as reason' (deliberative willing, boulesis), ever contrary to the Divine will, according to Aquinas?
options: No; while His sensuality and His 'will as nature' could shrink from things (like death) that God willed for Him, His will as reason always willed in accordance with the Divine will, as shown in Gethsemane's 'not as I will, but as Thou wilt'
Yes, His will as reason regularly opposed the Father's will throughout His ministry
No, because Christ's human will as nature never differed from the Divine will either
Yes, because Aquinas holds Christ had no rational will distinct from His sensuality
P4Q18.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes sensuality and will-as-nature (which naturally shrink from painful things like death, even things God wills) from will-as-reason (deliberative choice), showing that in His will as reason Christ always willed what God willed, illustrated by His words in Gethsemane.

P4Q19.q: Regarding the heresy that held 'one operation' in Christ (Monoenergism), what analogy does Aquinas use to explain the heretical view, and how does he ultimately respond?
options: The heretics compared the Godhead moving the manhood to a soul moving a body's inferior parts (one operation of the moving principle, with different things operated); Aquinas instead holds there are distinct human and divine operations proper to each nature, even while Christ acts as one
The heretics and Aquinas fully agree that there is strictly and simply one operation in Christ with no distinctions needed
Aquinas rejects any analogy between soul/body and Godhead/manhood as wholly inapplicable and useless
Aquinas holds there are three operations in Christ, one for each Person of the Trinity
P4Q19.explanation: Aquinas explains the Monoenergist analogy (soul as sole 'operator' moving the body's parts, yielding one operation with diverse effects) but distinguishes it from the orthodox view he defends: since Christ has two complete natures each with its own operative principle, there are properly two operations (divine and human), even though the person acting is one.

P4Q19.q: How could Christ's human actions be meritorious for Him, according to Aquinas, given that all good ultimately comes from God?
options: While God is the first cause of all good by authority, a creature can still be a secondary cause of possessing good by cooperating with God, and having something by one's own merit (even as secondary cause) is more excellent than having it without merit
They could not be meritorious in any sense, since all merit is excluded once grace is presupposed
They were meritorious only because Christ's human nature acted entirely independently of any divine causality
Merit is impossible in Aquinas's system for any rational creature, divine or human
P4Q19.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes God as the first cause 'by authority' of all good from the creature's role as secondary cause when it cooperates with God; having a good by such secondary, cooperative causation counts as having it 'of oneself' in a qualified sense, making merit possible and more excellent than possessing a good without merit.

P4Q20.q: In what threefold sense does Aquinas say Christ, in His human nature, is 'subject' to the Father?
options: Subject in degree of goodness (human nature participates rather than equals Divine goodness), in power (subject to Divine ordinance like any creature), and in His own will's act of obedience (obedient unto death)
Subject only in a single sense: bodily weakness relative to the Father's omnipotence
Subject only because the human nature was created after the divine nature temporally
Not subject in any real sense; 'subjection' language is purely metaphorical poetry with no theological content
P4Q20.explanation: Aquinas identifies a threefold subjection natural to any creature which Christ's humanity shares: participated (not equal) goodness, subjection to God's providential ordinance, and free obedience of will, the last exemplified by His obedience 'unto death' (Philippians 2:8).

P4Q20.q: Can it be said that Christ is 'subject to Himself,' per Aquinas?
options: Not if this implies two separate persons (one ruling, one serving) — that is condemned Nestorian heresy; but it can be rightly said with reference to the diversity of natures within the one Person, who rules according to His divine nature and serves/obeys according to His human nature
Yes, without qualification, since Aquinas fully endorses the Nestorian formula that the Word is Lord of the Man Christ
No, under no interpretation whatsoever can such language be used, even about the two natures
Yes, because Aquinas holds there really are two separate hypostases in Christ
P4Q20.explanation: Aquinas rejects the Nestorian sense (two persons, one commanding, one obeying) as heretical, but allows the phrase 'the Son is less than Himself' (following Augustine) when understood of the one Person considered according to His two distinct natures — ruling as God, serving as man.

P4Q21.q: Why, according to Aquinas, does it belong to Christ to pray at all, given that His Divine will is inherently effective?
options: Because Christ also has a distinct human will, which of itself is not efficacious enough to accomplish what it wishes except by Divine power, so prayer belongs to Him precisely as man with a human will
Because His Divine will alone prays, requesting help from the Father
Because prayer in Christ is purely symbolic and has no real basis in a distinct human will
Because Christ's human nature had no will of its own, so 'prayer' merely names the Father's own internal deliberation
P4Q21.explanation: Aquinas reasons that if Christ had only the Divine will, prayer would be pointless since the Divine will is automatically effective; but because His human will is really distinct and not of itself sufficient to accomplish its desires, praying belongs to Christ according to His human will.

P4Q21.q: When Christ prayed that 'the chalice' of His Passion might pass from Him, which will was expressing itself, according to Aquinas?
options: His sensuality and His simple will considered as nature (naturally shrinking from suffering), not His deliberate rational will, which He submitted fully to the Father's will
His sensuality alone, since His rational will had no capacity for such a prayer
His deliberate will as reason, meaning He definitively did not want to undergo the Passion at all
The Divine will itself, momentarily hesitating about the plan of redemption
P4Q21.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes Christ's sensuality/will-as-nature (which naturally recoiled from suffering and prayed accordingly) from His will-as-reason (deliberate, rational willing), which always concurred with the Father's will, as shown by His conclusion 'not as I will, but as Thou wilt.'

P4Q21.q: According to Aquinas, was every prayer of Christ literally granted?
options: Yes for what He willed absolutely (by reason's deliberation, i.e. will-as-reason); but requests arising merely from sensuality or will-as-nature were more like conditional 'velleities,' not absolute willing, and need not be granted as such
No, none of Christ's prayers were ever answered, since He was already in full possession of all good things
Yes, every request from every level of His will, including sensuality, was granted without exception
Aquinas declines to address whether Christ's prayers were heard
P4Q21.explanation: Aquinas explains that what is willed absolutely (per reason's deliberation) is truly willed and is granted, while what arises merely from sensuality or will-as-nature is a conditional 'velleity' rather than an absolute act of will, and thus is not simply granted as prayer in the full sense.

P4Q22.q: Why is it fitting, according to Aquinas, that Christ be called a priest?
options: Because the office of a priest is to be mediator between God and the people, bestowing divine gifts on them and offering their prayers and satisfaction to God, both of which Christ perfectly accomplishes
Because Christ literally served in the Jerusalem Temple's priestly rotation
Because 'priest' is merely an honorary title with no real mediating function attributed to Christ
Because Aquinas denies Christ can properly be called a priest at all
P4Q22.explanation: Aquinas defines the priestly office as mediation — bestowing divine gifts on the people and offering the people's prayers/satisfaction to God — and shows Christ fulfills both aspects perfectly, bestowing grace (2 Peter 1:4) and reconciling humanity to God (Colossians 1:19-20).

P4Q22.q: Does the effect of Christ's priesthood (expiation) extend to Christ Himself, in Aquinas's view?
options: No; as the fountainhead of the entire priesthood, Christ communicates the effect of priesthood to others without Himself needing or receiving it, just as the sun gives light without receiving it
Yes, Christ needed His own priesthood to expiate personal sin, just like any other priest
Yes, but only partially, since He still needed grace from the Old Law's priesthood
Aquinas holds the question is undecidable from Scripture
P4Q22.explanation: Aquinas argues that a priest normally needs a mediator because he cannot approach God on his own, but Christ 'comes of Himself to God' (Hebrews 7:25); as the source of the entire priesthood, He gives its effect to others without receiving it Himself, comparable to the sun which gives but does not receive light.

P4Q22.q: Why is Christ's priesthood described as 'according to the order of Melchisedech' rather than the Levitical order?
options: Because Melchisedech's priesthood, which received tithes even from Abraham (ancestor of the Levitical priests), prefigures the excellence of Christ's true priesthood over the merely figurative Levitical priesthood, which could not wash away sins or last forever
Because Melchisedech and Christ were biologically related through Abraham's lineage
Because the Levitical priesthood was itself eternal and needed no higher fulfillment
Because Aquinas denies any real typological connection between Melchisedech and Christ
P4Q22.explanation: Aquinas explains that the Levitical priesthood was a mere figure falling short of the reality (it could not remove sin and was not eternal), while Melchisedech, who received tithes from Abraham (in whose loins Levi was, in a sense, already tithed), foreshadows the surpassing excellence of Christ's true and eternal priesthood.

P4Q23.q: How does Aquinas explain divine 'adoption' in relation to human adoption?
options: God, out of infinite goodness, admits rational creatures to the inheritance of beatitude, but exceeds human adoption because God's grace actually makes the adoptee worthy of the inheritance, rather than merely selecting one already worthy
Divine and human adoption are identical in every respect, including the adopter selecting an already-worthy heir
Divine adoption means God merely names an heir without any transformation of the adoptee
Adoption applies only metaphorically to God and has no real theological content
P4Q23.explanation: Aquinas notes human adopters choose someone already worthy to be heir, but God's adoption is superior because His grace itself makes the person worthy of the heavenly inheritance he is admitted to, rather than presupposing worthiness.

P4Q23.q: Why, according to Aquinas, can Christ Himself not be called an 'adopted' Son of God, even in His human nature?
options: Because sonship belongs properly to the person/hypostasis, and Christ's only hypostasis is the uncreated Person who is God's Son by nature; one cannot participate in (be adopted to) what one already has essentially
Because adoption is reserved exclusively for angels, not any human nature whatsoever
Because Christ actually is called an adopted son throughout the article, contrary to how the question is often summarized
Because Aquinas holds Christ had no human nature capable of being called 'son' in any sense
P4Q23.explanation: Aquinas reasons that sonship belongs to the hypostasis, not merely the nature, and since Christ's sole hypostasis is the eternal Person who is naturally God's Son, He cannot also 'participate' via adoption in a sonship He already possesses essentially and by nature.

P4Q24.q: In what sense does Aquinas affirm that Christ was 'predestined'?
options: The union of the two natures in the Person of Christ, though eternally decreed by God, is something accomplished in time through grace, and so properly falls under predestination, understood as God's eternal preordaining of what will be done in time by grace
Predestination applies to Christ's Divine Nature itself, which was predestined to exist
It does not apply to Christ at all in any sense, since predestination applies only to sinners needing grace
Christ was predestined only in the sense that His birthplace was foreordained, not the union of natures itself
P4Q24.explanation: Aquinas defines predestination as God's eternal preordaining of things to be accomplished in time by grace; since the union of the two natures in Christ (God becoming man) is exactly such a temporal accomplishment through the grace of union, it properly falls under and is described by predestination.

P4Q24.q: Is Christ's predestination the cause of the predestination of the rest of humanity, according to Aquinas?
options: Not on the part of the single eternal act of predestining (one act covers both), but yes on the part of its term/effect, since God decreed our salvation to be achieved specifically through Christ
Yes entirely, since Christ's predestination temporally precedes and causes ours in every respect
No in every sense; Christ's predestination and ours are wholly unrelated
Aquinas declines to address any causal relationship between the two predestinations
P4Q24.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the single, simultaneous act by which God predestines both Christ and the rest of humanity (in this sense Christ's predestination isn't the cause of ours) from the ordained content or term of that decree, in which our salvation's arrangement 'through Jesus Christ' means Christ's predestination is causally prior with respect to how our salvation is achieved.

P4Q25.q: How does Aquinas explain that Christ receives both 'latria' (worship due to God alone) and 'dulia' (veneration due to creatures) without contradiction?
options: One and the same Person of Christ is adored with latria on account of His Divinity, and with dulia on account of His perfect humanity (viewed as adorned with grace), since adoration of His flesh as united to the Word is itself latria
Latria and dulia are simply synonyms in Aquinas's usage, so there is no real distinction
Christ receives dulia alone, since latria is reserved strictly for the Father
Christ's humanity receives no veneration whatsoever, only His divinity does
P4Q25.explanation: Aquinas explains that adoring Christ's flesh as the flesh of the incarnate Word is itself an act of latria (like honoring a king by honoring his robe as his), while venerating the humanity specifically for its perfection in grace is dulia — yet both terminate in the one adored Person.

P4Q25.q: Why does Aquinas conclude that images of Christ should be adored with latria, the same worship given to Christ Himself?
options: Because the mind's movement toward an image, insofar as it is an image (not merely as a carved or painted object), is one and the same movement as that directed to the thing it represents
Because the wood or paint of the image itself possesses inherent divine power
Because Aquinas actually denies any adoration is due to images, contrary to common misreadings
Because images of Christ are living relics equivalent to His literal body
P4Q25.explanation: Following the Philosopher's distinction of two mental movements toward an image (as a thing in itself, versus as representing something else), Aquinas argues that no reverence is due to the image as mere wood or paint, but reverence as image is identical to reverence for what it represents — hence the same latria given to Christ is given to His image.

P4Q25.q: What form of worship does Aquinas assign to the Blessed Virgin Mary, and why?
options: 'Hyperdulia' — a higher degree of dulia than given to other creatures, because latria is due to God alone and Mary remains a mere (though highest) rational creature
'Latria,' the same worship as given to God, since she is the Mother of God
'Dulia' identical in degree to that given to any canonized saint, with no distinction for her divine motherhood
No worship whatsoever, since Aquinas denies any veneration is owed to her
P4Q25.explanation: Aquinas reasons that latria belongs to God alone, and since Mary — despite her unique dignity as Mother of God — remains a mere rational creature, she is owed dulia, but a heightened form ('hyperdulia') exceeding that given to other creatures on account of her singular dignity.

P4Q26.q: Why, according to Aquinas, is Christ 'as man,' rather than as God, properly called the Mediator between God and men?
options: A mediator must be distant from each extreme yet unite them by communicating what belongs to one to the other; as man, Christ is distant from God by nature and from men by grace/glory, and can communicate divine gifts to men, which cannot be said of Him as God
Because as God He is closer to men than as man, making mediation trivial in that role
Because His divine nature communicates nothing whatsoever to His human nature
Because Aquinas denies Christ can be called Mediator in any sense, contrary to Scripture's own language
P4Q26.explanation: Aquinas explains a mediator must both be a mean, distant from both extremes, and unite them by communication; as God, Christ shares the very same nature and dominion as the Father and Spirit (so distance and one-way communication don't apply), but as man He is genuinely distant from God by nature and from men by dignity of grace/glory, and can truly unite them by communicating gifts and offering satisfaction and prayer.

P4Q26.q: Does Aquinas hold that Christ is the sole and perfect Mediator of God and men?
options: Yes, because He alone, through His death, perfectly reconciled the human race to God, uniting the extremes by giving Himself as redemption for all
No, he holds there are multiple equally perfect mediators, including Moses and the angels
Yes, but only in a merely honorary or titular sense with no real reconciling function
No, Aquinas denies the title 'Mediator' can properly apply to Christ at all
P4Q26.explanation: Aquinas affirms Christ alone is the perfect Mediator, since through His death He alone accomplished the reconciliation of humanity to God, citing 2 Corinthians 5:19 and 1 Timothy 2:5-6 ('who gave Himself a redemption for all').

P4Q27.q: Why does Aquinas argue that the Blessed Virgin's sanctification could not have occurred before the infusion (animation) of her rational soul?
options: Sanctification is the cleansing from original sin, which requires grace, and grace can only be received by a rational creature, which does not yet exist before the soul is infused
Because sanctification requires a fully formed body only, with the soul being irrelevant
Because Scripture explicitly states the exact hour of her ensoulment, ruling out prior sanctification
Because Aquinas denies she was ever sanctified in the womb at all
P4Q27.explanation: Aquinas reasons that sanctification (cleansing from original sin) requires grace, whose only possible subject is a rational creature; since the rational soul is not present until animation, sanctification logically cannot occur before that point.

P4Q27.q: According to Aquinas, why was it fitting that the Blessed Virgin receive an especially great fulness of grace in her sanctification?
options: Because the nearer a thing is to the source/principle of an effect, the more it shares in that effect, and Mary was nearest to Christ (the principle of grace) in His humanity, since He received His human nature from her
Because she performed extraordinary ascetic works of merit before her sanctification, earning greater grace
Because all human beings receive an equal, undifferentiated share of grace regardless of proximity to Christ
Because Aquinas denies Mary received any special grace beyond that of ordinary believers
P4Q27.explanation: Aquinas applies the principle that nearness to a causal source yields a greater share of its effects; since Christ is the principle of grace and Mary is nearest to His humanity (as the one from whom He received His human nature), she was due a greater fulness of grace than others.

P4Q27.q: Why does Aquinas hold that the Blessed Virgin, though sanctified in the womb, was preserved from all actual sin throughout her life?
options: Because God fittingly equips those chosen for a particular office to fulfill it worthily, and her office as Mother of God required freedom from sin, given the honor reflected between parent and child, her intimate bond with Christ, and the indwelling of Divine Wisdom in her
Because it was logically impossible for any human being to sin after any degree of sanctification
Because Scripture explicitly narrates a moment-by-moment account of her sinlessness
Because Aquinas concludes she was capable of actual sin but simply never had the opportunity to commit any
P4Q27.explanation: Aquinas reasons from the principle that God equips those He chooses for an office to fulfill it (2 Corinthians 3:6), and argues that the honor reflected between mother and child, her intimate association with Christ, and the indwelling of Divine Wisdom in her, made it fitting she remain free from all actual sin.

P4Q28.q: On what basis does Aquinas insist Christ's Mother remained a virgin in the very act of giving birth, not just in conceiving?
options: It befit the nature of the one born — the Word of God, which proceeds from the mind without corrupting it — that His body likewise be born of an incorrupt virgin, showing that body to be truly the body of the Word
Because ancient Roman law required unmarried mothers for all legitimate imperial claims
Because virgin birth was a common and unremarkable occurrence attested elsewhere in Scripture
Because Aquinas holds this claim to be theologically optional, a pious but non-binding opinion
P4Q28.explanation: Aquinas draws an analogy to how a mental word proceeds from the mind without corrupting it; since Christ is the substantial Word of God made flesh, it was fitting that His birth in the flesh likewise leave His mother's virginity intact, manifesting the nature of the One born.

P4Q28.q: How does Aquinas argue against Helvidius's claim that Mary bore other children after Christ?
options: Among other reasons, it would be derogatory to Christ's perfection, since as He is the Father's Only-Begotten in His Godhead, it was fitting He also be His Mother's only, perfect offspring in His humanity
Aquinas actually agrees with Helvidius that Mary bore several other children
Aquinas argues purely from Roman inheritance law to refute Helvidius, without theological grounds
Aquinas dismisses the question as unanswerable from available sources
P4Q28.explanation: Aquinas rejects Helvidius's claim (that Joseph and Mary had normal marital relations and other children) partly on the ground that it would diminish Christ's perfection: as He is the Father's only Son in His divine nature, it was fitting He remain His Mother's only child as well.

P4Q29.q: According to Aquinas, why was it fitting for Christ to be born of a virgin who was nonetheless legally espoused (betrothed/married) to Joseph?
options: For Christ's own sake (to avoid being deemed illegitimate by unbelievers), for Mary's sake, and for our sake — multiple reasons converge on the fittingness of an espoused virgin mother
Because espousal was legally required by Roman civil law for any valid birth record
Because Aquinas holds virginity and marriage are mutually exclusive, so espousal was a late correction of an earlier error
Because Joseph needed a legal claim to inherit Mary's family property
P4Q29.explanation: Aquinas lists reasons touching Christ Himself (avoiding the appearance of illegitimacy, e.g., so unbelievers could not fairly accuse Him), as well as reasons for Mary and for the wider community, all converging on the fittingness of her being an espoused virgin.

P4Q29.q: Did Aquinas consider the marriage between Mary and Joseph to be a 'true' marriage, despite their vow of virginity?
options: Yes; true marriage requires the first perfection (an inseparable union of souls / mutual pledge) which they had, even though the second perfection ordinarily achieved through intercourse was foregone by mutual consent
No, since without consummation there can be no true marriage under any circumstances
Yes, but only because canon law of Aquinas's own era redefined marriage to exclude consummation entirely
No, Aquinas denies any real marital bond existed between them, treating it as a mere legal fiction
P4Q29.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the 'first perfection' of marriage (the inseparable bond of souls constituting its essential form) from the 'second perfection' (its operation/end, achieved partly through intercourse); Mary and Joseph possessed the first perfection fully, making theirs a true marriage even without consummation.

P4Q30.q: Why did Aquinas think it was necessary for an angel to announce the conception of Christ to Mary beforehand, rather than it simply occurring?
options: To preserve a fitting order in the union of the Son of God with the Virgin — that she be informed in mind and freely consent before conceiving in the flesh, since (per Augustine) she is more blessed for bearing Christ in her heart by faith than in her flesh
Because Mary was entirely unaware of the plan of salvation and needed basic religious instruction
Because angels are required by Aquinas's system to announce every human conception without exception
Because the announcement was purely a formality with no bearing on Mary's own knowledge or consent
P4Q30.explanation: Aquinas, citing Augustine, argues it was fitting that Mary receive the mystery in faith/mind before conceiving in the flesh, showing that her spiritual reception of Christ (belief) is even more blessed than her bodily motherhood, hence the prior Annunciation was necessary to this proper order.

P4Q30.q: Why, according to Aquinas, was it fitting that specifically an angel (rather than, say, a direct unmediated event) announce the Incarnation to Mary?
options: It maintained God's established order whereby divine things are communicated to humanity through the ministry of angels, as elsewhere in salvation history (e.g., Gabriel also announcing John the Baptist's birth to Zachary)
Because angels alone are capable of physical speech, unlike God
Because Mary could not have believed a message from any other source
Because this order applies uniquely to Mary and to no other biblical annunciation
P4Q30.explanation: Aquinas appeals to the general order established by God (per Dionysius) whereby angels first receive and then communicate divine mysteries to humans, noting the parallel of Gabriel's role in announcing both John the Baptist's birth to Zachary and Christ's conception to Mary.

P4Q31.q: Why does Aquinas hold that Christ's flesh had to be derived from Adam (via Mary) rather than freshly created?
options: Because Christ assumed human nature precisely to cleanse and heal it, and human nature needed healing specifically as it was corrupted through its tainted descent from Adam, so the very nature that fell had to be the one assumed and healed
Because there was no other matter available anywhere in creation from which to form a body
Because Adam's flesh, unlike Mary's, was entirely free of any taint requiring healing
Because Aquinas denies any real biological connection between Christ and Adam
P4Q31.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since the purpose of assuming human nature is to heal its corruption, and that corruption specifically arises from tainted descent from Adam, it was fitting that Christ's flesh be derived from that same Adamic stock in order for the nature itself to be healed by the assumption.

P4Q31.q: According to Aquinas, what supplied the matter for Christ's conception, given that a supernatural (not human/male) power was the active principle?
options: The Virgin's blood, brought by her generative power to a stage of secretion apt for conception — the same kind of matter any woman naturally supplies, even though the active principle was the supernatural power of God rather than a man
Ordinary human flesh and bone taken directly from Mary's body
Matter brought down from heaven, not derived from Mary at all
No matter was involved; Christ's body was purely spiritual until the Nativity
P4Q31.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the natural element of Christ's conception (the matter, Mary's blood brought to a state fit for conception, just as in ordinary generation) from the supernatural element (the active principle being God's power rather than a human father), concluding Christ's body was conceived from this same kind of maternal matter.

P4Q31.q: Did Aquinas think Christ 'paid tithes in Abraham's loins' the way Levi is said to have done, per Hebrews 7?
options: No; if Christ had paid tithes in Abraham as Levi did, His priesthood would not be superior and 'according to the order of Melchisedech' but merely of the lower Levitical order, which is precisely what the Apostle's argument excludes
Yes, exactly as Levi did, since both descended bodily from Abraham in the same way
Yes, but only symbolically, with no bearing on the argument about priestly order
Aquinas declines to answer, treating the question as unanswerable
P4Q31.explanation: Aquinas reasons that the Apostle's argument for the superiority of Melchisedech's (and so Christ's) priesthood depends on Levi, but not Christ, having been 'in the loins' of Abraham when tithes were paid; therefore Christ did not pay tithes in Abraham as Levi did, preserving the higher, non-Levitical order of His priesthood.

P4Q32.q: Why is Christ's conception especially attributed to the Holy Ghost, even though the whole Trinity effected it?
options: Among other reasons, because the Holy Ghost is the mutual Love of the Father and Son, and the Incarnation itself flowed from the exceeding love of God for the world (as in John 3:16)
Because only the Holy Ghost, and not the Father or Son, possesses the power to act in creation
Because the Father and Son were entirely inactive during the conception of Christ
Because Scripture never actually attributes the conception to the Holy Ghost, contrary to the Creed
P4Q32.explanation: Aquinas explains that though the undivided Trinity acted, the conception is fittingly appropriated to the Holy Ghost as the personal Love of Father and Son, since it was out of God's supreme love that the Son took flesh (John 3:16).

P4Q32.q: Why does Aquinas deny that the Holy Ghost should be called Christ's 'father' with respect to His humanity?
options: Because sonship in the proper sense requires likeness to the generator, and Christ is the Son of God in the fully perfect sense only through His eternal generation from the Father, so applying 'sonship' improperly (via His human generation) to the Holy Ghost would misapply a term already used in its most proper sense elsewhere
Because the Holy Ghost had no causal role whatsoever in Christ's conception
Because Aquinas actually affirms the Holy Ghost should be called Christ's father, contrary to common summaries
Because 'father' and 'son' language cannot apply to Persons of the Trinity under any circumstances
P4Q32.explanation: Aquinas reasons that Christ is the Son of God in the perfect and proper sense solely through His eternal generation from the Father; since a term used properly in one sense should not also be used improperly of the same subject, Christ should not be called 'Son' of the Holy Ghost (or of the whole Trinity) with respect to His human generation.

P4Q33.q: Why does Aquinas insist Christ's flesh was assumed by the Word in the very same instant it was conceived, not conceived first and assumed afterward?
options: If the flesh had existed even momentarily before assumption, it would have had its own hypostasis distinct from the Word, and the Word's Incarnation would then involve destroying that pre-existing hypostasis — contrary to the very nature of the union, which unites human nature to the Word from the start
Because Church tradition simply forbids speculation on the timing without giving a philosophical reason
Because Aquinas holds the flesh was assumed centuries before being conceived, reversing the usual order
Because the soul, unlike the flesh, was assumed only after birth, making simultaneity irrelevant
P4Q33.explanation: Aquinas argues that positing a temporal gap between conception and assumption would require Christ's flesh to have first subsisted in its own hypostasis, which the Word would then have to displace or destroy upon assuming it — a scenario contrary to the very nature of the hypostatic union, hence contrary to faith.

P4Q33.q: In what sense does Aquinas call Christ's conception both 'natural' and 'miraculous'?
options: Natural with respect to the matter supplied by His Mother (which followed the ordinary pattern), but miraculous with respect to the active power that caused it (God's power replacing a human father); since form/activity take precedence in judgment over matter/passivity, the conception is described simply as miraculous
Entirely and exclusively natural, with no miraculous element whatsoever
Entirely and exclusively miraculous, with the maternal matter itself being supernaturally created from nothing
Neither natural nor miraculous, but a third, unrelated category unique to Christ alone
P4Q33.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the material element (Mary's contribution, ordinary/natural) from the active/efficient element (God's supernatural power in place of a human father, i.e. the form/activity), and since judgment follows what is more formal and active, the conception is properly termed miraculous overall, though natural in a certain respect.

P4Q34.q: According to Aquinas, did Christ have full use of free will and could He merit, already in the very first instant of His conception?
options: Yes to both; ultimate spiritual perfection lies in operation (not mere habit), and since intellectual/volitional acts are instantaneous (unlike bodily development), Christ had both the use of free will and true merit from the first instant, since His sanctification was for the sake of sanctifying others and thus by His own meritorious act, not merely a passive infant-like sanctification
No to both; Christ's use of reason and merit developed gradually just as with ordinary infants
Yes to free will's use, but Aquinas denies any possibility of merit occurring at the first instant
No, since Aquinas holds Christ possessed no human will capable of merit at any point
P4Q34.explanation: Aquinas reasons that operations of intellect and will are instantaneous acts of an already-perfect being (unlike bodily growth, which is gradual), and that Christ's sanctification, being of the more perfect adult type (by His own act rather than merely by another's faith, as with infants), included both use of free will and a truly meritorious movement of that will from His conception's first instant.

P4Q34.q: Was Christ, from the very first instant of His conception, already a 'comprehensor' actually seeing the Divine Essence, according to Aquinas?
options: Yes; since He received grace 'not by measure,' exceeding even the grace of the comprehensors, and it was unfitting that He receive merely habitual grace without its corresponding act, He was in act a comprehensor seeing God's Essence from the first instant
No, He only became a comprehensor gradually over His lifetime, culminating at His Ascension
No, He remained purely a wayfarer throughout His earthly life with no beatific vision until death
Yes, but only in a merely potential, not actual, sense throughout His life
P4Q34.explanation: Aquinas connects this to Christ's unmeasured fulness of grace (John 3:34): since grace received without an accompanying act would be incongruous with such fulness, and wayfarer's grace is by nature less than a comprehensor's, Christ must have possessed comprehensor-grace in full act — the beatific vision — from the first instant of His conception.

P4Q35.q: Why does Aquinas assign nativity (being born) to the person/hypostasis rather than to the nature as such?
options: Because 'to be born,' like 'to be generated,' properly pertains to what subsists, i.e. the hypostasis/person, since nature (a form) is only said 'to be' insofar as something subsists by means of it
Because nature is more fundamental than hypostasis in every possible respect
Because 'nativity' in Aquinas's system applies only to non-rational creatures, not persons at all
Because Aquinas denies nativity can be predicated of Christ in any sense
P4Q35.explanation: Aquinas reasons that being born, like being generated, terminates in being (esse), which properly belongs to what subsists — the hypostasis or person — rather than to the nature/form, which 'is' only in the sense that something subsists through it; hence nativity is attributed to the person, not the nature as such.

P4Q35.q: Why does Aquinas conclude it is heretical to deny that Mary is truly the 'Mother of God'?
options: Because the word 'God' can stand for the one hypostasis possessing both natures, and since that hypostasis (the Word) took human nature to Himself from the very first instant of conception, whoever conceived and bore that human nature conceived and bore God Himself, whatever the errors of Photinus or Nestorius might claim
Because 'Mother of God' is merely an honorary title Aquinas considers theologically optional
Because Mary literally generated the Divine Nature itself, apart from any question of hypostasis
