Because Aquinas holds the human nature existed independently before being joined to the Word, making 'Mother of God' technically inaccurate but pastorally useful
P4Q35.explanation: Aquinas argues that since a concrete term like 'God' can stand for the hypostasis (which possesses both divine and human natures), and that hypostasis was united to the human nature from the very moment of conception (not after, as Photinus or Nestorius would have it), Mary — who conceived and bore that hypostasis in its human nature — is truly and properly the Mother of God.

P4Q36.q: Why did Aquinas think it was NOT fitting for Christ's birth to be made known to absolutely everyone right away?
options: Because widespread immediate recognition of Christ's identity would have hindered the redemption accomplished through the Cross, since (per 1 Corinthians 2:8) if the 'princes of this world' had known Him, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory
Because Christ's birth was, in Aquinas's view, actually meant to remain permanently hidden and unknown to anyone at all
Because publicizing the birth would have violated Roman law regarding unregistered infants
Because there is no theological reason at all; Aquinas treats it as an arbitrary historical accident
P4Q36.explanation: Aquinas reasons that had Christ's identity and birth been made universally and immediately known, this would have obstructed the redemptive plan, since (citing 1 Corinthians 2:8) full recognition by the rulers of the world would have prevented the crucifixion necessary for salvation.

P4Q36.q: According to Aquinas, why were the birth-announcement recipients so varied — shepherds (Jews, lowly) via angels, and Magi (Gentiles, powerful/wise) via a star?
options: To foreshadow that Christ's salvation concerns all sorts and conditions of people (Jew and Gentile, lowly and powerful), with each group being led to Christ through signs suited to what was already familiar to them (angelic apparitions for Jews, celestial observation for Gentile astrologers)
Because angels can only appear to Jews and stars can only be understood by Gentiles, as a matter of metaphysical law
Because Aquinas holds the Magi account is purely legendary and theologically insignificant
Because shepherds and Magi were the only two categories of people alive at the time
P4Q36.explanation: Aquinas explains that Christ's universal salvation (Colossians 3:11/Galatians 3:28) is prefigured by manifestation to contrasting groups — righteous and sinners, lowly and powerful, Jew and Gentile — each reached through a mode of sign familiar to them: angelic apparition for Jews accustomed to receiving the Law via angels, and a star for Gentile astrologers.

P4Q36.q: Why does Aquinas (following Chrysostom) argue that the star of Bethlehem was not an ordinary star of the heavenly system?
options: Because of its anomalous course (north-south, unlike other stars), its visibility at midday, its intermittent appearing/hiding, its non-continuous stop-and-go movement matching the Magi's travel needs, and its descending low enough to indicate a specific house
Because Scripture explicitly states in so many words that it was an angel disguised as a star
Because Aquinas holds all Old and New Testament stars are always symbolic and never literal astronomical objects
Because contemporary Persian astronomers of Chrysostom's time denied any star existed at all
P4Q36.explanation: Aquinas draws on Chrysostom's several reasons that the star was not a natural celestial body: its unusual direction, its appearance at midday, its appearing and disappearing, its non-continuous motion synced to the Magi's travel, and its descending to indicate a specific house — concluding it was likely some rational power made visible under the form of a star.

P4Q37.q: Aquinas lists several reasons Christ should have been circumcised. Which of the following captures one of his central reasons?
options: To prove the reality of His human nature against those (Manicheans, Apollinarius, Valentine) who denied it was truly ordinary human flesh, and also to show His approval of the divinely instituted rite and His descent from Abraham
Because circumcision was required for Christ's Davidic royal claim under Roman law, unrelated to any theological purpose
Because Christ's circumcision was purely accidental and carried no doctrinal significance for Aquinas
Because Aquinas denies Christ was actually circumcised, treating the Gospel accounts as symbolic
P4Q37.explanation: Among Aquinas's several reasons: circumcision proved the reality of Christ's true flesh against docetic-type heresies, showed approval of the Old Law's rite, confirmed His Abrahamic descent, removed a Jewish objection to accepting Him, gave an example of obedience, and let Him take on the Law's burden in order to free others from it.

P4Q37.q: Why did the Blessed Virgin, though not herself subject to the Law's purification requirement (since her conception was virginal and sinless), go to the Temple to be purified?
options: To imitate Christ's own humility and obedience in submitting to legal burdens He was not bound by, to show approval of the Law, and to avoid giving the Jews an excuse for calumny — the same reasons Christ Himself submitted to circumcision
Because she was, in fact, subject to the ordinary purification law like any other Jewish mother, with no special exemption
Because Roman civil law compelled her attendance regardless of Jewish religious law
Because Aquinas denies she ever went to the Temple for purification at all
P4Q37.explanation: Aquinas parallels Mary's Temple purification with Christ's circumcision: neither was strictly bound by the Law's demands, but both submitted for the sake of humility, example, approval of the Law, and to remove any pretext for Jewish criticism.

P4Q38.q: According to Aquinas, did John's baptism itself confer sanctifying grace?
options: No; John's baptism, like the work of a servant preparing matter for the master-craftsman, only prepared the way for grace (through teaching faith in Christ, accustoming people to baptism's rite, and penance), while grace itself came only through Christ
Yes, John's baptism was fully equivalent in grace-giving power to Christ's baptism
No, John's baptism accomplished nothing at all, being a purely empty ceremonial gesture
Yes, but only for Gentile converts, not for Jews
P4Q38.explanation: Aquinas compares John's role to a servant preparing matter for the master-craftsman's form; since grace comes through Christ (John 1:17), John's baptism did not itself confer grace but prepared people for it through teaching, ritual familiarization, and penance.

P4Q38.q: Why did Aquinas think it was fitting that John's baptism continue even after Christ Himself had been baptized, rather than ceasing immediately?
options: Stopping abruptly might suggest jealousy or anger toward Christ, would have given Christ's own disciples cause for greater envy, allowed John to keep directing hearers toward Christ, and matched the principle that the 'shadow' of the Old Law should not withdraw until the truth was fully manifest
Because John was legally obligated by Jewish law to continue baptizing for a fixed additional period
Because Aquinas holds Christ's baptism was actually inferior to John's and needed John's ongoing ministry to remain valid
Because there is no reason at all; Aquinas treats the continuation as a mere historical accident with no theological significance
P4Q38.explanation: Aquinas (citing Chrysostom and Bede) gives several reasons for the continuation: avoiding the appearance of jealousy, preventing greater envy among Christ's disciples, John continuing to direct hearers to Christ, and the fittingness that the 'shadow' of the Old Law not withdraw before the full truth was manifest.

P4Q39.q: Since Christ had no sin needing washing, why, according to Aquinas, was it fitting for Him to be baptized?
options: To sanctify/consecrate the waters of baptism for others by His sinless flesh, to bequeath sanctified water to future recipients, and to fulfill 'all justice' by first doing Himself what He commanded others to do, thereby setting an example
Because Christ actually did possess personal sin requiring cleansing, contrary to standard Christian teaching
Because baptism was legally mandated for all Jewish men regardless of sinlessness
Because Aquinas holds Christ's baptism was purely ceremonial theater with no deeper purpose
P4Q39.explanation: Aquinas (citing Ambrose, Chrysostom, and Augustine) gives multiple reasons: Christ purified the waters rather than being purified by them, He bequeathed sanctified water to later baptism, and He fulfilled 'all justice' by exemplifying obedience to what He commanded others to do.

P4Q39.q: Why was it fitting, according to Aquinas, that Christ be baptized specifically with John's water baptism rather than a baptism 'in the Spirit'?
options: Because Christ did not need spiritual baptism, having been filled with the grace of the Holy Ghost from the first instant of His conception; being baptized with John's baptism also showed approval of it and further sanctified baptism itself by His example
Because John's baptism was in fact greater and more spiritually potent than any baptism 'in the Spirit'
Because Christ was incapable of receiving any spiritual gift, including the grace of the Holy Ghost, before His Passion
Because Aquinas denies Christ was baptized by John at all, contrary to the Gospel accounts
P4Q39.explanation: Aquinas explains that since Christ already possessed the fulness of the Holy Ghost's grace from His conception, He had no need of the spiritual effect John's baptism prepared for; instead, His acceptance of John's water baptism showed approval of it and sanctified the rite of baptism by His own submission to it.

P4Q39.q: Why does Aquinas hold that the dove in which the Holy Ghost appeared at Christ's baptism was a real, not merely imaginary, dove?
options: Because just as it did not befit the Son (the Truth) to use anything unreal (hence a real body, not an imaginary one), so it did not befit the Holy Ghost (the Spirit of Truth) to deceive by using a merely apparent form; God, who forms a real human body from nothing, could easily form a real dove
Because Scripture explicitly states the dove was later kept alive as a relic by the apostles
Because Aquinas holds the Holy Ghost was permanently and personally united to the dove, similarly to the hypostatic union
Because Aquinas actually denies the dove was real, treating it as purely symbolic/visionary
P4Q39.explanation: Aquinas draws a parallel between Christ's true body (fitting for the Son as Truth) and the Holy Ghost's real dove (fitting for the Spirit of Truth): neither Person would fittingly use a merely apparent, deceptive form, and God's power that formed a true human body without human seed could just as easily form a real dove.

P4Q40.q: Why did Aquinas conclude Christ should live among people publicly rather than pursue a solitary/hidden life?
options: Because Christ came into the world specifically to bear witness to the truth and preach openly (John 18:37), so a hidden, solitary existence would have worked against the very purpose of His Incarnation
Because solitary living was against Jewish law at the time and would have been illegal
Because Aquinas holds Christ actually lived as a hermit for most of His adult life, contrary to the Gospels
Because public life was required to accumulate the wealth needed for His mission
P4Q40.explanation: Aquinas reasons from the purpose of the Incarnation itself — to testify to the truth and preach openly, as Christ says of Himself in John 18:37 — concluding that a hidden, solitary life would be unfitting to that mission, so He lived and preached publicly among people.

P4Q40.q: Why did Aquinas hold it fitting for Christ to live in poverty rather than wealth?
options: Because His preaching mission required freedom from worldly cares of wealth (as He instructed the apostles not to carry gold or silver), so that all His time and attention could be devoted to preaching, unencumbered by managing possessions
Because poverty was religiously mandated for all first-century Jewish teachers without exception
Because Christ actually possessed considerable wealth throughout His ministry, according to Aquinas's reading of the Gospels
Because Aquinas holds material wealth is inherently and always sinful for any person to possess
P4Q40.explanation: Aquinas connects Christ's poverty to His preaching mission: since preachers devoted fully to God's word must be free from the burdens of wealth management (as Christ instructed the apostles, Matthew 10:9), it was fitting that Christ Himself model this freedom from worldly possessions.
